The White-browed brushfinch (Arremon torquatus) is a Neotropical passerine that undergoes a rapid pre-natal developmental period. Neonates emerge at a very modest body mass of only 4.34 grams [Ww0 = 4.34 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves characteristic of species that rely heavily on biparental provisioning from the moment of hatching. This initial wet weight stands in marked contrast to the substantially greater masses achieved later in life, highlighting the steep growth trajectory the species must sustain during the early nestling phase. The nestlings are entirely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and food delivery during the first days following emergence, with the female brooding extensively while the male shuttles arthropod prey to the nest.

As the developing chicks progress through the pin-feathered nestling stage, a critical developmental milestone is the achievement of flight. The first successful breeding event, however, is deferred considerably beyond this physiological threshold. The time since birth at first brood is 401.5 days [tR = 401.5 days] under the same thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a substantial delay that is likely imposed by the need to acquire a breeding territory and achieve sufficient body condition before committing to reproduction. This lag between the attainment of sexual maturity and actual first reproduction is a common life-history pattern among long-lived passerines inhabiting competitive, saturated environments.

Adult body mass exhibits a modest degree of sexual dimorphism in the White-browed brushfinch, consistent with a socially monogamous mating system where both sexes contribute to nesting duties. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches 40.75 grams [Wwi = 40.75 grams], a figure that may be elevated during the breeding season due to the development of reproductive tissues and the storage of calcium for eggshell formation. These asymptotic masses are achieved gradually over the first year of life, with the growth curve decelerating markedly as individuals approach their final adult size during the subadult period.

Maximum recorded longevity in the wild is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] under the standard thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a figure derived from long-term mark-recapture studies in the species' high-altitude Andean range. Seasonal breeding is timed to coincide with periods of peak insect abundance, ensuring that the demanding nestling and fledgling phases coincide with maximal food availability.
